title: What the government does in an economy

blocks.heading: What this section asks of you
blocks.text: Identify the jobs the government does in an economy, explain why it does them, and discuss how far its role can reach.

blocks.heading: What the government does
blocks.text: The government is the authority that runs a country. In an economy its role is to provide public goods and services that firms tend not to find profitable to sell - street lighting in Oshakati lights everyone who passes, and buyers tend to wait for a neighbour to pay rather than paying themselves - to raise revenue through taxes on income and spending, to transfer some of that revenue to households through payments such as the old-age pension, to regulate the markets that firms and consumers trade in, and to manage the economy as a whole toward aims such as jobs and steady prices. The German city of Hamburg runs its water supply the same way: one public provider, one set of pipes, funded from public revenue.

blocks.heading: Why the government steps in
blocks.text: Why does the government do these jobs rather than leave them to markets? Start where a market works: two traders exchange because each gains. Then notice what the market cannot do. Because buyers who do not pay still enjoy street lighting, a firm selling it collects from a few and serves many, so providing it tends to be unprofitable. Where one seller grows so dominant that buyers lose choice, it may raise prices above what a competitive market would charge, so the government regulates it. And where income divides very unequally, a government that judges this unfair can redirect resources through taxes and pensions. Each government function traces to something the market alone does not deliver, which is why the role of government differs from country to country and from year to year.

blocks.heading: How far the role reaches
blocks.text: The role is wide, not unlimited. In Namibia the government runs schools, pays the old-age pension out of tax revenue, licenses banks and inspects taxis; in the Netherlands the government spends close to half the country's yearly output, while in a poorer country the same list is shorter. The boundary is not fixed. A very poor country may lack the revenue to pay pensions on a wide scale - revenue limits it. Taxes raised too high may push a business toward shutting or moving - the activity shrinks, and with it later tax revenue. Running an industry, as with a national airline, requires skill and information a government may lack, so it is likely to run some industries less well than a firm with market experience. So a government widens its role where it can raise revenue and run the task, and narrows it where it cannot - the role moves with capacity.

blocks.heading: The boundary in a real situation
blocks.text: In 2026 the small farms of the Kavango valley have no all-weather road to the market in Rundu. No single trader gains enough from a road to build it, so none is built. The government may build it because every farm gains and so do shoppers in Rundu, so it uses public revenue to build what no single buyer would. People react, too: if the money comes from a new levy on the same farms, some farmers would rather keep their earnings and wait; if a trucking firm lobbies for the levy to fall on its rival's goods, the rule may help that firm while leaving shoppers worse off. There is also a limit: where the valley's next project costs more than the region can raise, the government cannot build it, and the want goes unmet. The example shows every side of the role: provider, taxer, regulator, and the boundary of what is possible.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The macroeconomic aims this role serves - jobs, steady prices, growth, balanced external trade and a fairer distribution of income - are unpacked in 4.2, and the fiscal and monetary tools a government uses to steer the whole economy are treated in 4.3 and 4.4. Topic 2.10 covers the market outcomes that trigger intervention in more detail.
